*****CALL FOR PROPOSALS*****DEADLINE THURSDAY, MARCH 8 ************

The University of Colorado and the University of Denver proudly welcome the political networks community to Boulder for the 5th Annual Political Networks Conference and Workshops.  The sessions will be hosted at the Wolf Law Building on the Boulder campus, June 13-16, 2012.  Proposals for posters, papers, panels, and funding (for graduate students and recent Ph.D.s) will be accepted through March 8th.  All materials (including letters of support) must be in at that time.

The first two days of the conference will include training workshops on social networks research, including an all-day introductory session for novices (Michael Heaney) and several concurrent sessions for intermediate and advanced networks scholars (led by Steve Borgatti, Carter Butts, James Fowler and others). Days three and four of the conference will be devoted to posters, panels, and plenary speeches by David Knoke and John Padgett.

To apply, please visit the website:

http://socsci.colorado.edu/~stwo0664/index.html
Please email: network.conference@colorado.edu<mailto:network.conference@colorado.edu>  with questions.

We hope to see you this summer!

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Modeling Advice
messages.body_plain:
Hello Users:

I'm writing to collect some general advice about modeling a particular type of data. I hope the following longish description of the current modeling puzzle is appropriate for this list, as it involves both theoretical questions and empirical specification questions. I have estimated a series of ERGM and Siena models in my attempt to explain the network variation in my data, but I have encountered numerous problems relating to degeneracy and model specification.  Ultimately, my goal is to appropriately model the relationships of actors in two different legislative institutions and test for the presence of bridging-ties.  Below, I describe my data, my hypothesis, and the modeling approaches I've attempted. I hope to gather some insight from the list about the most appropriate method for testing the claims of interest.

The data are from two legislative bodies (US and EP).  In the US case, we have three time periods/waves, and in the EP we have two waves (total of 5 adjacency matrices).  The dependent variable describes the relationships between legislative actors through legislative member organizations (LMOs). We have a number of dyadic and nodal attribute variables as well about the actors.  The hypothesis I seek to test is whether there are bridging-ties among the legislators through their LMO memberships.  We have no hypotheses across the US and EP--only within legislature hypotheses.

One approach I've tried is to simply calculate betweenness (in the SNA package) for each network of legislators in each time period, add this as a vertex attribute, and estimate an ERGM, in which betweenness is a nodal-covariate, in addition to a series of other endogenous structural terms and exogenous covariate controls.  I can do this 5 times--one ergm for each legislative time period. For example:

mymodel1<-ergm(cauc109.aff.dichot.net~edges+triangle+density+twopath+nodecov("between")+nodematch("party")+nodematch("statecode")+nodematch("gender")+nodematch("leader")+nodematch("black")+nodecov("term")+nodecov("electpct"), eval.loglik=TRUE, seed=123, interval=1000, burnin=100000, MCMCsample=1000000, verbose=T)

However, these models have difficulty with convergence and fit.  I am unable to obtain MCMC standard errors, and even after numerous attempts at respecification the diagnostics suggest that fit may be problematic.  Note that every run of a model takes a number of hours on a high memory machine so there is a limit to the number of iterations I can do.

Another approach is to use Siena.  Siena should allow me to take advantage of the longitudinal nature of the data (even though in the EP we only have two waves--which is limiting for Siena).  I have been able to estimate some Siena models using these data; however, suspicions about correlations between structural terms have forced me to reduce the model quite a bit.  The EP models I have run are very pared down and still suggest problems with degeneracy and fit.  The US models have yet to converge after running for several days on the high memory machine.  Experts on the Siena list have warned me about correlations and wondered if Siena was the appropriate architecture for these data.

For example, I have tried the following effects:
> myeffus
   effectName                        include fix   test 
1  constant caucuses rate (period 1) TRUE    FALSE FALSE
2  constant caucuses rate (period 2) TRUE    FALSE FALSE
3  degree (density)                  TRUE    FALSE FALSE
4  betweenness                       TRUE    FALSE FALSE
5  same usstate                      TRUE    FALSE FALSE
6  same usparty                      TRUE    FALSE FALSE
7  same usblack                      TRUE    FALSE FALSE
8  same uswomen                      TRUE    FALSE FALSE
9  usterm similarity                 TRUE    FALSE FALSE
10 uselectpct similarity             TRUE    FALSE FALSE

So my various attempts at testing this hypothesis using these advanced methods have left me frustrated.  While we can (and have) tested the idea using a variety of less sophisticated methods, it seems to me that the advanced statistical methods, such as those available through ERGM and Siena, are designed for exactly this type of modeling; however, I have not been able to achieve satisfactory findings that are reportable. I can continue to try to reparameterize the models to search for fit and to avoid degeneracy, but I would like to hear thoughts of readers of this list regarding:
- the appropriate method for testing the hypothesis
- best practices for iterative modeling and specification for these types of models (given that each iteration is so computationally expensive)
- which architecture (ERGM, Siena, something else?) seems most appropriate for the data

I am happy to collect responses off-list and post a summary to the list later if there is sufficient discussion on some of these items.  I can also provide additional helpful details off list.

Best,
Jennifer Victor


Jennifer N. Victor
Assistant Professor of Political Science
University of Pittsburgh
4600 Posvar Hall
jnvictor@pitt.edu
(412) 624-7204

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Modeling Advice
messages.body_plain:
Jennifer

I'm confused about what you are trying to model.  You say you want to
determine if there are bridging ties, but to answer this would not require
an ERGM or SIENA model.  I would ask which ties act as bridging ties and
measure their extent of bridging.  Then I would calculate edge betweenness
to see which ones are in bridging positions  and see if this varies over
time.  If you want to know which nodes act as bridges then you can calculate
betweenness or bridging and see which people are bridges.

-Tom

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Interaction effects between node attributes
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statneters,

I have some questions about interaction effects between node attributes. I
hope that you can help me with this.  I already read earlier discussions on
interactions, but they do not deal with my problem exactly.

 

Assume the following: The network to be predicted is directed; the nodes
have one metric attribute X, ranging from 0 to 1. The theory that I use
predicts an interaction, so that when both nodes i and j are high in X, i
becomes more likely to direct a tie at j. However, when either i or j are
low in X, this likelihood should decrease.

 

I implemented this interaction effect between Xi and Xj with a matrix that
stores the products of  Xi and Xj for all pairs of nodes (named XiXj ). My
final model looks like this (plus some other terms):

 

model<- ergm(network ~ edges + nodeicov (X) + nodeocov (X) +  dyadcov
(XiXj))

 

My questions are: 

 

1)      Is this model specified correctly?

2)      More specifically: 

a) When I include the interaction term, do I always have to include the
icov/ocov terms (just as I should include the main effects when testing
interaction effects in linear regression models)?

b) Should I include the interaction matrix as an edge-covariate or as a
dyad-covariate?

c) In my results table (see below), the estimated parameters for the
interaction terms are very high. I explain this as follows: I know that Xj
is an important predictor of the tie from i to j (i.e. when X is included
only as nodeicov/nodeocov, the estimated parameters are 5.46/-0.48). Yet,
the distribution of X among the nodes is right-skewed (with a mean of  .14
and maximal value of .8). Thus, after multiplication, the values in the
cells of the interaction matrix are rather small (typically < .10). Based on
this, in my interpretation, the results indicate that there is an
interaction effect between XiXj and the high parameter estimates for this
effect are due to the small values in the interaction matrix. Do you think
my interpretation is correct or do the high values indicate there is
something wrong with the model?

messages.subject: [statnet_help] error simulating bipartite networks with networksis
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] error simulating bipartite networks with networksis
messages.body_plain:
Dear users,

I'm trying to simulate bipartite networks from my dataset of 67 actors and 20 events. I did import the data in matrix form and create the object of the class network as bipartite. If I call my network, the output information is exactly the same as if I call the sample network 'finch'. Something as follows:

> bip1
 Network attributes:
  vertices = 87 
  directed = FALSE 
  hyper = FALSE 
  loops = FALSE 
  multiple = FALSE 
  bipartite = 67 
  total edges= 186 
    missing edges= 0 
    non-missing edges= 186 

 Vertex attribute names: 
    vertex.names

However, when using the command "simulate" on my data I got the following error, which doesn't happen when running it on the data sample finch

> simulate (bip1, nsim=1)
Error in mat[row.sums > 0, 1:ncol.nonnull] <- matrix(s$newmat, ncol = ncol.nonnull) : 
  number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length

When looking on the help files, I notice that the author set an attribute for nodes to identify to which class they belong. I did so too, despite even if you can run simulate (finch, nsim=100) without doing it; and still get the same error. 

On the other hand, I'm also interested on modeling the coincidences of my actors on the events. On the help file there seems to be a way but my computer crashes when running the help code, even when reducing the number of simulations:

data(finch)

## Simulate graphs and record the networks statistics ##
## specified by 'coincidences(x)'                     ##
sim<-simulate_sis(finch~coincidences(0:17), nsim=10000)

Have anyone else run into the same problems?

I'd appreciate any help to better understand the error and avoid it when performing simulations. 

Best wishes,

Juan Rocha
PhD student
Stockholm Resilience Centre
Stockholm University

Dear Hamid,

Sorry about the slow reply. The BIC computed is based on the theoretical
development by Handcock, Rartery, and Tantrum (2007), and I am not 100%
sure, off the top of my head, how well it translates to AIC.

As it is, the quickest way would probably be to take the BIC, take away
the p*log(n) part and add in the 2*p part.

(In your model, nstats is more than 5000.)

Hope this helps!
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] error simulating bipartite networks with networksis
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] error simulating bipartite networks with networksis
messages.body_plain:
Dear Juan,

The problem is that 
simulate(bip1, nsim=1) 

doesn't provide enough information by itself.  To use simulate.network, you'll need to provide information about a model class and the specific parameter values that identify a particular member of that class.  Said member define a probability distribution on the set of all networks, which is something from which one can logically simulate.  So, for instance:

simulate (bip1~edges) # This gives a formula, but still no parameters (however, the ergm package will use 0 as the default parameter).

simulate (bip1~edges, coef=1) # This gives a formula, identifying a model class (ERGMs whose sufficient statistic is the number of edges) as well as a coefficient value.  

Hope this helps.

Best wishes,
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Philip.  I don't know of any easy way to do it, but one possibility is to concatenate the 8 matrices into a single 80x11 matrix, then read this in using read.table, convert it to a matrix using as.matrix, and finally convert it to a 10x8x11 array using
a <- array(my_80x11_matrix, dim=c(10,8,11))

You can then access, say, the 3rd 10x11 sub-matrix using a[,3,].  As for computing the distance matrix, I think you'd want to use the apply function for this purpose.

Best,
Dave

messages.subject_clean: AW: [statnet_help] Fitting ergm with sender and reciever fails
messages.body_plain:
Dear Arne,

> after playing around with maxNumDyadTypes it seems like my model is
> too complex to converge. Nevertheless, I'm trying to avoid memory
> problems by using a HPC-Cluster (nodes with 64GB Ram) at the moment,
> but do not have any outcome yet.

There is also a problem with your model being

edges + isolates + sender + receiver

Having, edges, sender, and receiver in it means that every vertex's
degree will be modeled exactly. This means that a degree distribution
term like isolates is going to be nonidentifiable, so this model can't
be fit.

> Maybe simplifying the network will help? My network uses multiplex
> edges, choosing only unique edges reduces the number of edges to
> 11.000. Is there a way to include edges weights (from multiple edges)
> into the ergms? The weights are stored in an edge attribute called
> "weight".

ergm doesn't handle multiplex edges at all, so I think that it's already
only looking at unique edges. As for edge weights, that functionality is
in the works, and we hope to release it sometime this year.

                  I hope this helps,
                  Pavel
